```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)

pacman::p_load('tidyverse', 'kableExtra', 'knitr')

baseColor <- '#4CA384'
accent1 <- '#9AD079'
accent2 <- '#C4C6C7'
accent3 <- '#19424C'

Mode <- function(x) {
  ux <- unique(x)
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(x, ux)))]
}


```

```{r, context = 'server'}
output$skewPlot <- renderPlot({
  set.seed(1022)
  normDat <- data.frame(X=rnorm(300, mean = 10, sd = 1))
  if(input$skew == 'Somewhat Negatively Skewed'){
    normDat$Y <- (normDat$X^5)*-1
  } else if(input$skew == 'Negatively Skewed') {
    normDat$Y <- (normDat$X^10)*-1
  } else if(input$skew == 'Positively Skewed') {
    normDat$Y <- (normDat$X^10)
  } else if(input$skew == 'Somewhat Positively Skewed') {
    normDat$Y <- (normDat$X^3)
  } else {
    normDat$Y <- normDat$X
  }
  
  normDat$Y <- as.vector(scale(normDat$Y))
  
  ggplot(normDat, aes(x = Y)) + 
    geom_histogram(data=normDat, aes(x=Y, y = after_stat(density)), fill = '#9AD079', color = '#19424C', binwidth = .4) +
    stat_function(fun=dnorm, geom = "line", args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linewidth = 1, color = '#19424C') +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-8, 8)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, .8)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mean(normDat$Y), color = '#4CA384', linewidth = 2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = median(normDat$Y), color = '#18778C', linewidth = 2) +
    annotate(geom='rect', xmin = 2, xmax = 3, ymin = .5, ymax = .52, fill = '#4CA384') +
    annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3.3, y = .51, label = 'Mean', size = 7, hjust = 0) +
    annotate(geom='rect', xmin = 2, xmax = 3, ymin = .4, ymax = .42, fill = '#18778C') +
    annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3.3, y = .41, label = 'Median', size = 7, hjust = 0) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          axis.title = element_blank())
    }, height = 400)

```

## Intro to Today's Lab

During today's lab, you'll apply some of the concepts discussed during this week's lecture and familiarise yourself with jamovi, the statistical software used on this course. Each lab consists of several tasks, with corresponding questions you can answer. Please note that the questions are not required and not marked, although they do provide a helpful source of formative feedback that will help you to gauge your understanding. 

#### **Learning Objectives**
At the end of this lab, you will be able to:

1.  Open data in jamovi
2.  Check and reset variable types and codes
3.  Produce plots that allow you to visually assess your data's distribution
4.  Check the descriptive statistics of your data



#### **Lab Overview**
In this lab, you'll be working with data collected from the RMAP course studies. This specific dataset contains variables that measure interpersonal relationships and general well-being. You'll use these data to generate descriptive statistics and visualisations.



```{r, echo = F}
dat <- read.csv('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/ExploringDataLabData.csv')

                      "Participant's estimate of the number of the past 30 days that their health was not good",
                      "Perceived social support item 1",
                      "Perceived social support item 2",
                      "Perceived social support item 3",
                      "Perceived social support item 4",
                      "Perceived social support item 5",
                      "Perceived social support item 6",
                      "Perceived social support item 7",
                      "Perceived social support item 8",
                      "Perceived social support item 9",
                      "Perceived social support item 10",
                      "Perceived social support item 11",

datInfo %>%

```

All MSPSS variables use the following levels:

  + 1 = Strongly Disagree
  + 2 = Disagree 
  + 3 = Somewhat Disagree
  + 4 = Neutral
  + 5 = Somewhat Agree
  + 6 = Agree 
  + 7 = Strongly Agree

## Open Data and Check Variables

In this course, jamovi will be used to perform the majority of the tasks. Today's data can be downloaded onto your device by <B>[clicking here](https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/ExploringDataLabData.csv)</B> or checking this week's folder on <b>[the course Learn page (requires university login)](https://www.learn.ed.ac.uk/)</b>.

Once data have been opened in jamovi, the *Variables* tab allows you to make adjustments to each variable's characteristics. Recall that data can be measured in multiple formats, and these scales of measurement may affect how data can be described and analysed. In *Variables*, this format can be adjusted. This is useful, as jamovi does not always properly identify the variable format. 

You can also label your variable levels in the *Variables* tab. This is useful when nominal data are coded numerically (e.g., 'No' = 0; 'Yes' = 1). When labels are added, it adds clarity to the values of nominal variables. It is important to always include a coding key, so that anyone who works with the data will know how to interpret the numeric labels used and can make appropriate interpretations. 

### Your Tasks
<div class="nobullet">
+ [ ] $\ $ Open 'ExploringDataLabData.csv' in jamovi.
+ [ ] $\ $ Review each Measure Type and make any necessary changes. 
+ [ ] $\ $ For ordinal variables, make sure the levels fall in the expected order.
+ [ ] $\ $ Add a key to the `MSPSS` variables so that 1 = 'Strongly Disagree', 2 = 'Disagree', 3 = 'Mildly Disagree', 4 = 'Neutral', 5 = 'Mildly Agree', 6 = 'Agree', and 7 = 'Strongly Agree'. 

</div>

```{r checkingData, echo = F}
quiz(caption = 'Check Your Understanding',
     question('Which label is used in jamovi to describe ratio data?',
              answer('Nominal'),
              answer('Ordinal'),
              answer('Continuous', correct = T),
              message = 'Data that are either ratio or interval should be set as Continuous in jamovi'),
     question('What type of data is the Ethnicity variable?',
              answer('Nominal', correct = T),
              answer('Ordinal'),
              answer('Scale'),
              message = 'Ethnicity is a categorical variable with no order. It is therefore considered to be nominal data.'),
     question('What type of data are each of the MSPSS items?',
              answer('Nominal'),
              answer('Ordinal', correct = T),
              answer('Scale'),
              message = 'Each MSPSS variable represents a single Likert-style response. They should be designated as Ordinal, as they have an inherent order, but there is otherwise no meaningful numeric relationship.')
    )
```

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>
<br>
<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Opening the Data </span>

Click the three horizontal lines, then click 'Open'. Navigate to the folder on your device where this week's data are stored and select the file.

<br>
<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Checking Variable Measures </span>

To check that the variables are labeled as the correct scale of measurement, select each variable in the *Variables* tab and look at the box labeled 'Measure type'.

jamovi labels the data as:

* **Nominal:** data that fall into discrete categories that have no information regarding order (e.g. eye colour)
* **Ordinal:** data that fall into discrete categories that have some kind of ordering information (e.g. Likert Scale responses)
* **Continuous:** continuous/numeric data; individual values have some kind of numeric relationship beyond order (e.g. reaction time in seconds).

The proper variable labels are:

  + `ID`: Nominal
  + `AgeBracket`: Nominal
  + `Gender`: Nominal
  + `Ethnicity`: Nominal
  + `HighestEducation`: Ordinal
  + `HRQOL1`: Ordinal
  + `HRQOL2`: Ordinal
  + All `MSPSS` variables: Ordinal
  + `HRQOL`: Ordinal
  + `PWB`: Continuous
  + `WEMWBS`: Continuous
  
<br>
<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Ordering Variable Levels </span>

By default, jamovi orders the levels of ordinal variables alphabetically. Variable levels often need to be reordered to reflect their conceptual order. For instance, in the photo below, 'Poor' should appear at the top, and 'Excellent appear at the bottom:

```{r, echo = F, out.width='75%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ExploringData_reorderLevels.png')
```

To reorder the levels into their meaningful order, navigate to the *Values* tab and click on an ordinal variable. Highlight the level you wish to reorder in 'Levels' box, then use the arrows to change its position.

<br>
<span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 14pt"> Adding Labels to Variables </span>

To associate a label with each value of a variable, navigate to the *Values* tab and click on a variable. Note that you can highlight multiple variables if you need to make an identical change.

Tick the boxes next to all MSPSS variables and then double-click the level you wish to change. A text box will appear, and you can add the associated label. Note that the original value will still be retained in smaller text in the same box. 

```{r, echo = F, out.width='75%', fig.align='center'}
include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ExploringData_changingLabels.png')
```

Once you've finished adding labels, click out of the box. If you've done this properly, you'll see that each numeric value is now associated with a character label.

</details>
</div>
</br>

## Computing Variables

Sometimes, you'll need to use your variables to compute a new value or variable (e.g., a composite score from subscores). jamovi can perform a wide range of calculations on the variables. In today's lab, the data includes the individual responses to the 12 questions that make up the Perceived Social Support scale (MSPSS), and you need to compute the total MSPSS score. 

### Your Task

<div class='nobullet'>
+ [ ] $\ $ Use each of the 12 MSPSS items (`MSPSS1` through `MSPSS12`) to compute a composite score that reflects their total sum.
+ [ ] $\ $ Name the new variable `MSPSStotal`
</div>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt">Click here for a hint </span></summary>

Use the *Compute* button in the *Data* tab to find the function you need.

</details>
</div>
</br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt">Click here for the solution </span></summary>

To compute a new value from a current column, navigate to *Data > Compute*. Type the name for the new variable (`MSPSStotal`) into the top box. Click in the function box next to the equal sign, then click the fx button, then scroll down to `MSPSS1` in the *Variable* box. Double-click to add it to the function box, add a '+', then add `MSPSS2`. Continue this process until all MSPSS variables are included in the formula. 

```{r, echo = F, out.width='75%', fig.align='center'}
include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ExploringData_computeVariables.png')
```

After completing the formula, you will have a new column that reflects the total Perceived Social Support score.

</details>
</div>

## Check Frequency Data

Before doing any sort of analysis, it's important to first check the data to make sure everything is as expected. With categorical data, one way we can do this is to inspect the frequency of observations in each group. This allows you to evaluate the following:

+ Are observations distributed relatively equally or are there major differences across groups?
+ Are there any groups with a limited number of observations?
+ Are there any missing datapoints?
+ Are there any values outside the expected range?

### Your Task
<div class="nobullet">
+ [ ] $\ $ Check the frequency of your nominal variables. Make sure to display frequency tables.
</div>

Are any of these groups limited in size? If so, consider how this might affect your ability to make generalisable claims about this group.

Use the frequency tables to answer the following questions:
```{r freqData, echo = F}
quiz(caption = '',
     question_numeric('How many missing datapoints are there on the Gender variable?',
              answer(93, correct = T),
              message = '93 participants are missing data on the HighestEducation variable.'),
     question_numeric('How many participants responded that their general health was fair?',
              answer(36, correct = T),
              message = '36 participants indicated that their general health was Fair.'),
     question_numeric('How many levels were included in the HighestEducation variable?',
              answer(3, correct = T),
              message = 'The HighestEducation variable had 3 levels: (1) Undergraduate Degree; (2) Postgraduate Qualification, Masters; (3) PhD or other professional qualification')
    )
```


<div class="container">

## Visualise Distribution of Data 

Another useful way to check variable distribution is to visualise the data. Depending on the data type, a bar chart or a histogram could be used.

```{r, echo = F, fig.width= 3.5, fig.height=2.5, message=F}
freqDat <- data.frame(Bar=sample(c('Yes', 'No', 'Maybe'), size = 30, replace = T, prob = c(.25, .25, .5)), 
                      Histogram=rnorm(30, mean = 10, sd = 4))

ggplot(freqDat, aes(Bar)) + geom_bar(fill = baseColor, color=accent3) +
  labs(x ='Bar Chart') +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14, face = 'bold'))

ggplot(freqDat, aes(Histogram)) + geom_histogram(fill = baseColor, color=accent3) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14, face = 'bold'))
  
```

If you ordered your variable as instructed in [Open Data and Check Variables](#open-data-and-check-variables), your plot will look like the above figure. If you did not, you can go back and reorder `HRQOL2` now and the plot will update automatically.

## Distribution & Central Tendency

When data are skewed, it can impact how well the measure of central tendency represents the sample. Use the plot below to see how different levels of skewness can impact the mean and median.

```{r, echo = F}
fluidRow(column(width = 4, 
                selectInput('skew', 'Choose a skewness level:', choices = list('Negatively Skewed', 'Somewhat Negatively Skewed', 'Normal', 'Somewhat Positively Skewed', 'Positively Skewed'))))

plotOutput('skewPlot')
```

```{r skewness, echo = F}
quiz(caption = '',
     question('Which value is higher when data are positively skewed?',
              answer('mean', correct = T),
              answer('median'),
              answer('They are about the same.'),
              message = 'When data are positively skewed, the mean is higher because it is impacted by the extremely high scores in the tail.'),
      question('Which value is higher when data are normally distributed?',
              answer('mean'),
              answer('median'),
              answer('They are about the same.', correct = T),
              message = 'When data are normally distributed, the mean and median will be similar to each other.')
    )
```


## Check Central Tendency & Measures of Variability

When preparing to perform analysis, one of the most important steps is to check the descriptive statistics of your variables. These values are useful summary metrics and may provide insight into patterns in your data.

### Your Tasks
For all continuous variables in your data:

<div class="nobullet">
+ [ ] $\ $ Check the appropriate measures of central tendency
+ [ ] $\ $ Check the standard deviation and maximum/minimum values.
</div>

```{r descriptives, echo = F}
quiz(caption = '',
     question('Which measure of central tendency should be used to describe WEMWBS?',
              answer('mean', correct = T),
              answer('median'),
              answer('mode'),
              message = 'WEMWBS is a continuous variable with a nonskewed distribution (as you noted in the "Visualise Distribution of Data" task). It should be described using the mean.'),
      question('Which measure of central tendency should be used to describe MSPSS?',
              answer('mean'),
              answer('median', correct = T),
              answer('mode'),
              message = 'MSPSS was negatively skewed, so the mean may be biased by the extreme scores on the low end of the distribution. It could be more accurately described using the median'),
     question_numeric('What is the standard deviation of the PWB score? Please round your answer to two decimal places.',
              answer(13.54, correct = T),
              message = 'The standard deviation of the PWB score is 13.54.'),
     question_numeric('What is the minimum MSPSS score?',
              answer(22, correct = T),
              message = 'The minimum MSPSS score is 22.')
    )
```


<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt">Click here for a hint </span></summary>

To get each of these descriptive statistics, navigate to *Analyses > Exploration > Descriptives*. Consider how the data's distribution should impact the measure of central tendency you will use to describe the variable.

</details>
</div>
<br>

<div class="container">
<details><summary><span style = "font-weight: bold; font-size: 16pt"> Click here for the solution </span></summary>
To get all 3 measures of central tendency, you'll need to select *Analyses > Exploration > Descriptives*, then put the variables of interest into the 'Variables' box. Click 'Statistics' and check that the options for 'Mean', 'Median', 'Std. Deviation', 'Maximum' and 'Minimum' are selected.

```{r, echo = F, out.width='75%', fig.align='center'}
include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ExploringData_descriptiveOptions.png')
```

Although continuous variables could be described using both mean and median, the mean is often the most appropriate when the data are not skewed. The median may be more appropriate when the data are skewed, as the median is less impacted by extreme scores. Data will be reported in table format in the output.

```{r, echo = F, out.width='75%', fig.align='center'}
include_graphics('https://mtruelovehill.github.io/PRM/Labs/images/ExploringData_descriptiveData.png')
```

</details>
</div>
</br>
